paper_title: Learning to Read Out: Unembedding Dynamics in Language Model Pretraining

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: When does a language model acquire a capability? Developmental studies usually answer this by tracking when models start producing the correct token. But that prediction passes through the unembedding matrix, or readout, which is itself still being learned during pretraining. We show that a model's hidden states can encode task information before its own readout expresses it, so timelines read from outputs conflate what the model encodes with what its readout expresses. To track the readout directly, we introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, which fits one sparse dictionary to every token's readout row at every checkpoint. Unlike crosscoders on activations, it needs only checkpoint weights. We use it to locate a narrow early window, 0.4-1.1% of the way through Pythia's pretraining, in which the readout reorganizes and WordNet word categories become decodable from its rows. By then, linear probes on the hidden states already decode task information that the model's own outputs do not yet show. To test whether such gaps depend on how fast the readout learns, we pretrain small models from scratch that differ only in the readout's learning rate. We find that raising it makes the readout develop earlier and the gap close sooner, with little effect on final loss. Together, these results imply that early in training, where many developmental transitions are dated, a behavioral date can reflect when the readout learns to express task information and not when the model learns it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Developmental studies of language models ask when model learns capability, and they often date it through the models outputs. Surprisal curves across checkpoints date when individual words are acquired [Chang and Bergen, 2022], and translation accuracy dates shift from copying to translation [Körner et al., 2026]. The same study traces this shift across layers with the logit lens [nostalgebraist, 2020], which reads hidden states through the unembedding. All of these measurements read the model through its readout, the unembedding matrix that maps the last-layer hidden state to vocabulary logits. The readout is itself learned during pretraining. For the prompt The keys to the cabinet, an early hidden state of Pythia-1B [Biderman et al., 2023] prefers the incorrect is under its own readout but the correct are under the final checkpoints readout, although the hidden state is the same (Figure 1a). The source of this discrepancy is the logit computation. For token with readout row wv and last-layer hidden state h, its logit is ℓv = wv, and between two checkpoints ℓv = wv + wv + wv. Checkpoint comparisons with the logit lens [Wang et al., 2024, Körner et al., 2026], vocabulary projections [Wiegreffe et al., 2025], or attention head scores computed through the readout [Tigges et al., 2024] share this ambiguity. The information task depends on, such as subject number when choosing are over is, is available once linear probe can decode it from the hidden state, and natively expressed once the models own readout prefers the correct answer. Probing studies measure the first [Tenney et al., 2019], and behavioral studies measure the second. Prior work has found related gaps between what model encodes and what it outputs. Trained models can encode more than their outputs express [Orgad et al., 2025, Gekhman et al., 2025], and during training, internal structure can form before the behavior it supports appears in the outputs [Chen et al., 2024, Nanda et al., 2023]. We show that the readout has its own developmental timeline, which shapes when available information becomes natively expressed. This matters most early in training, where developmental transitions are dated [Olsson et al., 2022, Chen et al., 2024, Körner et al., 2026], and where the readout reorganizes, consistent with the early organization of vocabulary embeddings [Papadimitriou and Prince, 2026]. To track the readout itself, we introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, crosscoder fit to readout weights rather than activations. Like sparse autoencoder [Bricken et al., 2023, Huben et al., 2024], it learns dictionary of directions, called features, and rebuilds every tokens row at every checkpoint from small fraction of them (Figure 1b). We also decode fixed hidden states with the readouts of other checkpoints (Figure 1a). We make the following contributions: 1. Problem. We formalize confound in behavioral dating that also affects evaluations of early checkpoints, with diagnostics that separate hidden state and readout contributions (Section 2.3). 2. Method. We introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, which decomposes the readouts development into sparse features that can be followed across checkpoints. Unlike crosscoders on activations [Bayazit et al., 2026, Ge et al., 2026], it needs only checkpoint weights and covers the full vocabulary (Section 2.1). 3. Readout dynamics. We identify narrow early window, 0.41.1% of the way through training, in which the Pythia readout reorganizes and WordNet categories become decodable from its rows (Sections 4.1 and 4.2). 4. Availability and expression. Hidden states of Pythia-1B and 6.9B encode subject number before the models own readout or any intermediate readout expresses it (Section 4.3). 5. Training intervention. We show that raising only the readouts learning rate in small controlled pretraining runs makes the readout develop earlier and native expression reach availability sooner, 2 with little effect on final loss. Early comparisons of training recipes can therefore reflect how fast the readout develops (Section 4.5).

sections.title: 2 Method
sections.content: We track the readouts development with parameter-trajectory crosscoding (Sections 2.1 and 2.2) and separate hidden state and readout contributions with probes and readout swaps (Section 2.3).

sections.title: 2.1 Parameter-Trajectory Crosscoding
sections.content: Dating the readouts development requires knowing which groups of tokens change, along which directions, and when. As training proceeds, each next-token loss pulls the targets readout row toward the hidden state and pushes every other tokens row away from it, so the rows of many tokens drift along shared directions [Gao et al., 2019, Bis et al., 2021]. We describe these shared motions with sparse dictionary, which rebuilds each tokens row at every checkpoint from small fraction of its learned directions, called features. Each feature is active for only some tokens, so unlike principal component it identifies group of tokens as well as direction, and token can belong to several groups. Sparse autoencoders fitted separately per checkpoint number their features independently, and matching them to follow feature through training is error-prone because dictionaries trained with different seeds learn partly different features [Paulo and Belrose, 2026]. We therefore adopt the crosscoder approach [Lindsey et al., 2024, Ge et al., 2026] and fit one dictionary to all checkpoints at once. Each token has one code per feature that is shared across checkpoints, and each feature has one decoder direction per checkpoint. features direction, norm, and active tokens can therefore change over training while its index stays fixed. We fit the dictionary to readout parameters rather than activations, so it needs only checkpoint weights, without labels or an activation corpus. We center and scale each checkpoints rows, so decoder norms exclude the growth of the mean row and of the readouts overall scale. sections.title: 2.2 Measuring Readout Development
sections.content: We describe each feature by its decoder norm trajectory D(t) 2 across checkpoints. To compare when features grow and decay rather than how large they are, we divide each trajectory by its maximum and classify it with fixed rules into one lifecycle profile, such as early-decaying, persistent, or late-emerging (Appendix D). To locate when the readout changes most, we measure six kinds of change between adjacent checkpoints, such as how much decoder norms change and how far decoder directions rotate. The reorganization score of window of training steps is the geometric mean of the six measures, each summed over the window and normalized, so it is high only where several kinds of change coincide. The reorganization window is the window whose score most exceeds circular-shift nulls, which shift each measure in time independently, keeping its own profile but breaking the alignment between measures (Appendix D.4). For the controlled runs of Section 4.5, we also report two simpler statistics. The median feature peak step is the median over features of the checkpoint at which each decoder norm peaks, and the peak turnover step is the checkpoint at which normalized decoder norms change most from the previous checkpoint.

sections.title: 3 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Models and dictionaries. We study readout development in Pythia-160M, 1B, and 6.9B [Biderman et al., 2023] and in OLMo-2-7B, which differs from Pythia in architecture, tokenizer, and training recipe [Team OLMo et al., 2025]. The dictionaries for all four models cover the full vocabulary across 32 public checkpoints (Table C.1). To test how the readouts own optimization shapes its development, we train four additional 31M-parameter models on the first 10B tokens of Pythias preshuffled training data, in Pythias order, from shared initialization (Section 4.5). Three runs differ only in the readouts learning rate multiplier (0.25, 1, 4), and the fourth keeps the 1 multiplier and halves the warmup from 1430 to 715 steps. Each 31M model is trained once, and three dictionaries with one shared width and sparsity weight are fitted to 16 of its checkpoints. Tasks and scoring. We compare readouts on binary tasks, each with correct answer token and foil  (Table 1)  . Subjectverb agreement (SVA) [Linzen et al., 2016, Marvin and Linzen, 2018] contrasts the agreeing verb form with the non-agreeing one, indirect object identification (IOI) [Wang et al., 2023] contrasts the recipient with the giver, and number comparison contrasts the correct number with the other number in the prompt. Labels are balanced by subject number, by whether the recipient is the first or second name, or by number order, and each answer is single token that includes its leading space. The native readout and each swapped readout are scored at the final prompt position with the margin of Equation (5). Contrast accuracy compares only the two answers and ignores every other token in the vocabulary. With balanced labels, its chance level is 50%. Probes and controls. We measure availability with linear probes on the final hidden state. For simple SVA and IOI in Pythia-6.9B, the probe is logistic regression, fit at each of the 32 checkpoints (Section 4.3). For broader suite of 20 task families, the probe is single direction from shrinkage linear discriminant analysis (LDA), fit on the families with shared binary label, and we call its accuracy A1 (Appendix F). Prompts that share noun, name pair, or number pair always fall in the same cross-validation fold. We compare each probe with three controls: probe at step 0 shows what is decodable before training, probe on prompt tokens alone tests whether surface features suffice, and probe on random Gaussian features tests whether the classifier fits unrelated inputs. Probes fit to shuffled labels stay below 0.56 on the availability sets of Table 1. Appendix A.3 gives fit details and maps controls to confounds. Sparse localization. To find which readout features carry task margin, we decode step-1000 Pythia-1B states with the dictionarys reconstruction of the final readout, which is how logit lens with the final readout reads an early checkpoint. The reconstructed readout is sum of feature contributions, so each feature contributes separate term to the margin, and features attribution is the mean of this term over items. He et al. [2026] explain logit lens scores this way for single readout. In this work, the features come from dictionary fitted across all 32 checkpoints, so each feature keeps the same index throughout training. For SVA, IOI, and greater-than completion  (Table 1)  , we keep only answer pairs whose rows in the final readout have similar norms, log(wy+2/wy 2) 0.5. This filter limits the effect of row norm on the margin. We split each tasks items into two equal 5 parts at random and select the eight features with the largest attribution on the first part. On the second part, we measure contrast accuracy under two edits to the reconstruction: ablation, which removes these features, and isolation, which keeps only them. We compare these edits with the full reconstruction and with the same edits applied to random features matched on decoder norm, firing rate, and attribution sign (Appendix G.4). Lexical organization. The dictionary dates when the readout reorganizes but not what its rows learn. To check this without the dictionary, we probe the readout rows directly for WordNet supersenses, broad categories such as nouns for animals [Miller, 1995, Fellbaum, 1998]. For each of the 35 categories with at least 20 whole-word tokens, we train one-vs-rest logistic probe on two-thirds of the centered readout rows and report its balanced accuracy (the mean recall over the two classes) on the remaining third. Three controls test whether token metadata (frequency, length, row norm, spacing, and token class) explains this accuracy. The first probes the metadata alone, the second probes matched random token sets, and the third shuffles labels within metadata bins (Appendix E).

sections.title: 4 Results
sections.content: We first ask when and how the readouts structure changes (Sections 4.1 and 4.2), then whether hidden states encode task information before the models own readout expresses it (Sections 4.3 and 4.4), and finally whether the readouts learning rate sets the timing of its development (Section 4.5). We first check how well the dictionaries reconstruct the readout, since the lifecycle and localization analyses read it through them. Across Pythia-160M, 1B, and 6.9B and OLMo-2-7B, the dictionaries explain 0.8080.920 of the variance in the readout trajectories. On average, each readout row uses 1.172.26% of the features at each checkpoint, and no feature is dead (Figure C.1). They also reconstruct Pythia-160M checkpoints held out from fitting nearly as well as the fitted ones (Appendix C.5). They nearly match the fit of sparse autoencoders fitted separately per checkpoint with far fewer active features, and unlike those autoencoders they keep one feature index across checkpoints. In Pythia, dense PCA needs far more components to reach the same fit (Appendix C).

sections.title: 4.1 The Readout Reorganizes Early
sections.content: When does the readout change, and do its features share one growth pattern? In all four models, the reorganization score peaks within the first few percent of training. In Pythia, it peaks between step 512 and step 1.6k in all three models, 0.4% to 1.1% of the way through training, window that contains the end of the learning rate warmup at step 1430. This window stands out against circular-shift nulls, with = 0.005 at 160M and 1B and = 0.04 at 6.9B (Figure 2, bottom; Figure D.2 and Table D.2). Of the 21 Pythia dictionaries we fitted, 20 select the same window and the remaining one selects the adjacent window (Appendix D.5). Measures of raw readout movement that use no dictionary, such as the drift of its top subspace, also put the largest movement early, at the checkpoint pair ending at step 256 or 512, just before this window (Figure C.6). In OLMo-2-7B, the score peaks at similar fraction of training, between step 9k and step 28k. This window lies 13% of the way through OLMos first training stage, the main pretraining phase before mid-training. It does not separate from the nulls (p = 0.12, Appendix D). Features do not share one growth pattern. We follow each feature by its decoder norm, which sets how far the feature moves its tokens logits. In Pythia-160M and 1B, some features peak early and decay, others persist, and others emerge late, while nearly all Pythia-6.9B features persist and most OLMo-2-7B features emerge late (Figures 2 and D.1). OLMo-2-7Bs readout also grows more gradually, with its total decoder norm rising through most of training. These profile shares vary with dictionary width and sparsity (Appendix D.5). Early decay also depends on the checkpoints nearest initialization. Pythia-1B dictionary fitted only from step 256 onward assigns 0.02% of its features to the early-decaying profile, against 24% in the main Pythia-1B dictionary (Appendix D.3). sections.title: 4.2 Lexical Organization Develops Alongside Structural Change
sections.content: Do the readout rows acquire recognizable lexical organization while their structure changes? In Pythia-160M, the median probe accuracy across the 35 WordNet categories rises from 0.499 at initialization to 0.874 at the final checkpoint. We call category decodable once its accuracy stays at or above max(0.55, acc0 + 0.05) for three successive checkpoints, which counts only gains above its accuracy at initialization. All 35 categories become decodable by step 1000, and 33 have their largest gain between steps 128 and 1000 (Figure 3). In Pythia-1B, the median category becomes decodable at step 512, with onsets from step 128 to step 2000 (Appendix E). We compare the probes with the three controls of Section 3. The first control, probe on token metadata alone, predicts some categories well early in training. From step 512 onward, median readout accuracy exceeds it. Against the second and third, by step 512, 33 of 35 categories exceed the 95th percentile of both the matched-random and the shuffled-label nulls, and by step 1000 all 35 do. Splitting the tokens into training and test sets by lemma, so that variants such as dog and Dog never appear in both, leaves the early rise unchanged and lowers late accuracy, to final median of 0.841 with 34 of 35 categories decodable by step 1000 (Appendix E). Lexical organization therefore emerges in the readout rows before and during the 5121.6k window.

sections.title: 4.3 Hidden State Availability Precedes Native Readout Expression
sections.content: Figure 4: Pythia-6.9B hidden states encode subject number before the models own readout or any intermediate readout expresses it. (a) Accuracy on simple SVA of the logistic probe, the native readout, and the best swept readout over intermediate checkpoints; the arrow marks the gap at step 512. (b) Single-direction probe A1 and native expression on the four agreement sets of Table 1 at the final checkpoint; annotations give A1 E, and bars are 95% Wilson intervals for E. Is task information decodable from the hidden state before the models own readout expresses it? probe and the native readout can disagree because they read the hidden state along different directions. The probe learns its direction from the task labels, while the native readout can only use the difference between its two answer rows. If the state separates the answers along direction that this difference does not yet point in, the information is available but not expressed. Expression begins once the hidden state or the readout changes so that the two directions line up. We track the probe, the native readout, and the oracle readout sweep on the same items at every checkpoint. On Pythia-6.9B agreement, the probe approaches ceiling by step 512 while native expression and even the best swept readout are still at chance (Figure 4a). Probes on prompt tokens and on random Gaussian features stay near chance, so neither surface tokens nor classifier fitting explains the probes accuracy (Figure F.1). The same early gap appears in every subjectverb agreement set of the broader 20-family suite whose probe starts near chance, in both Pythia-1B and Pythia-6.9B (Appendix F). Can later readout decode the current hidden state better than its own? For next-token prediction, it can. On Wikipedia text in nine languages, the step-1000 readout lowers the aggregate next-token loss of Pythia-1B step-256 and step-512 states by 1.50 and 0.15 nats, and every language prefers an intermediate readout, even after aligning the two readouts frames (Figures G.1 and G.3 and Table G.1). Early in training, the readout therefore lags behind the hidden states. The final readout also raises early task accuracy, from 0.800 to 0.925 on Pythia-1B step-1000 SVA states, as in Figure 1a, but this gain depends on its frame and falls to 0.566 after an orthogonal Procrustes alignment [Schönemann, 1966], which rotates the final readout to best match the native one (Appendix G.4). Availability therefore precedes native expression. Section 4.4 asks which readout directions carry these margins, and Section 4.5 tests whether the readouts own optimization sets their timing.

sections.title: 4.4 A Few Readout Directions Carry the Agreement Margin
sections.content: Which parts of the readout carry task margin? In the localization setup of Section 3, eight features carry the SVA margin. Ablating them lowers reconstructed SVA accuracy from 0.900 to 0.487, keeping only them gives 0.938, and ablating matched random features leaves 0.931. These interventions are causal evidence that the reconstructed final readouts SVA margin on step-1000 states runs through these eight directions. Appendix G.4 repeats the analysis for IOI and greater-than completion. This analysis decomposes the logit lens margins of Section 4.3 into readout features.

sections.title: 4.5 Readout Learning Rate Shifts Readout Development
sections.content: Early in training, the readout lags behind the hidden states, and in Pythia its reorganization window contains the end of warmup. Does the readouts timing come from how fast the readout itself learns, 8 Figure 5: faster readout develops earlier and lowers early validation loss, while final losses agree within 0.06 nats. (a) Median feature peak step and peak turnover step against the readout learning rate multiplier; bars span the three fits where they differ, and dashed circles mark the shorter warmup. (b) Validation loss of each 31M run minus that of the baseline run. or from its warmup? We find that changing the readouts learning rate shifts when its features peak, while halving the warmup leaves this timing unchanged on our checkpoint grid. In the 31M runs of Section 3, raising the multiplier moves the median feature peak step from 128 to 64 to 32 in every fit (Figure 5), one checkpoint per fourfold increase. Halving the warmup leaves the median feature peak at its baseline value in every fit. faster readout also lets native expression reach availability sooner. In these runs, availability is probes accuracy on the frequency class of the next token, and native expression is the models accuracy on the same classes. Along the multiplier axis, slower readout gives larger early gap between this probe and native expression, and the gaps close by step 1024 in every run except 0.25, which closes by step 2048. Readout swaps show the same ordering. In the 0.25 run, step-256 hidden states are decoded best by the step-512 readout, which lowers their next-token loss by 0.91 nats and keeps this gain after orthogonal Procrustes alignment, whereas in the 4 run each checkpoints own readout is best (Appendix H.4). Does developing earlier leave the model better off at the end of training? It lowers early loss but not final loss. At 0.27B tokens, the validation loss of the 4 run is 1.20 nats below the baseline and 2.08 nats below the 0.25 run, whereas final validation losses agree within 0.06 nats (Figure 5b). We therefore identify the readouts learning rate as one factor that shifts when the readout develops and when native expression reaches availability. Unlike the fixed-state swaps of Section 4.3, this intervention acts during training and changes the hidden states as well as the readout.

sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Reading development through the readout. Developmental analyses track linguistic representations, circuits, and concepts across checkpoints [Olsson et al., 2022, Nanda et al., 2023, Inaba et al., 2025, Xu et al., 2024, Sawmya et al., 2025], and the logit lens and tuned lens project hidden states into vocabulary scores [nostalgebraist, 2020, Belrose et al., 2023]. Analyses that read development through the outputs depend on readout that is itself still being learned. We add the readout to these comparisons, tracking its rows with shared sparse features and testing how changing it alters what fixed hidden states express (Table I.1 compares these approaches). Weight-space analyses. Analyses of output embeddings study weight tying [Inan et al., 2017, Press and Wolf, 2017], the softmax bottleneck [Yang et al., 2018], and embedding geometry and its evolution [Gao et al., 2019, Machina and Mercer, 2024]. Closest to our lexical analysis, Papadimitriou and Prince [2026] correlate the geometry of input and output embeddings with semantic, syntactic, and frequency structure over training. Parameter decomposition and weight-sparse models analyze mechanisms in weights, typically at one model state [Braun et al., 2025, Gao et al., 2026]. As an alternative to reading logit lens scores in token units, He et al. [2026] explain them as sums of sparse feature contributions, decomposing single readout from its weights alone. 9 Shared dictionaries over checkpoints. Sparse autoencoders decompose activations into sparse features [Bricken et al., 2023, Huben et al., 2024, Templeton et al., 2024, Gao et al., 2025, Rajamanoharan et al., 2024a], and crosscoders share feature indices across layers or models [Lindsey et al., 2024]. The closest methods are the checkpoint crosscoders of Bayazit et al. [2026] and Ge et al. [2026], which learn shared features over activations sampled from text corpus (400M and 800M tokens) and relate their evolution to behavior through interventions or attribution. We adopt their shared codes and checkpoint-specific decoders, with the gate and sparsity penalty of Ge et al. [2026], both of which use decoder norms, and apply them to token-aligned readout parameters. Fitting then needs only checkpoint weights and covers every readout row rather than only the tokens corpus elicits, while the behavioral tests still need text, forward passes, and task labels.

sections.title: 6 Discussion
sections.content: Taking our findings together, we argue that the readout is part of the measurement in any analysis that reads development off logits. rise in output accuracy or in logit margin can come from the hidden state or from the readout, even for continuous scores that avoid metric-induced emergence [Schaeffer et al., 2023]. Reporting native expression, probe on the same task with its initialization baseline, and readout sweep on the same states would help distinguish the two. Readout change concentrates in the same early period in which many developmental transitions are dated [Chen et al., 2024]. The induction head phase change, for example, occurs roughly 12% of the way through training in large models [Olsson et al., 2022], close to the 0.41.1% window in Pythia. behavioral date in this period can therefore reflect readout development as well as hidden state development. What drives the different feature trajectories within this period remains open. Language models first predict from unigram frequencies and then loosely from bigram probabilities, before converging on richer predictions [Chang and Bergen, 2022], and early-decaying features may record the first of these stages, with late-emerging features taking over as context use develops. The same confound affects evaluations of early checkpoints and of small, briefly trained models, which inform forecasts of how larger runs will perform [OpenAI, 2023, Snell et al., 2024]. Such forecasts already contend with capabilities that appear abruptly with scale [Wei et al., 2022, Ganguli et al., 2022]. While the readout still lags, outputs can underreport what the hidden states already encode, whereas probe alone would overpredict expression. Internal progress measures can anticipate behavioral transition [Nanda et al., 2023]. Testing whether native expression, probes, and readout sweeps sharpen such forecasts, also for safety-relevant capabilities, is natural next step. The lag is largest early in training. Once the readout has reorganized, each hidden state is decoded best by its own readout or neighbor, and native expression catches up with availability on several tasks, so most implications concern analyses of early checkpoints. In the 31M runs, the readouts learning rate changes early loss and when distinction becomes expressible, but leaves final losses within 0.06 nats (Section 4.5). Recipe comparisons made on partial runs can therefore reflect how fast the readout develops rather than where training ends. Overall, learning representation and learning to express it can happen at different times in pretraining, and measuring both separates what model encodes from what its logits express. Limitations. First, limited compute restricted the evidence that the readouts learning rate shifts its timing to one 31M setting, with one run per condition stopped at 10B tokens. The readout holds about 42% of the parameters there, against about 10% in Pythia-1B, so larger models remain untested. Second, availability is measured with probes on two-token contrasts, so the gap describes when binary distinction becomes expressible, not when an open-ended capability appears. Appendix I.2 covers further limits, such as checkpoint density and dictionary settings. Future work. We suggest three useful directions. First, recipe comparisons on early checkpoints can favor faster readout even when final losses agree (Section 4.5). Checking whether recipe rankings made with probes or swapped readouts match the final rankings would test fix. Second, extending pretrained models vocabulary adds untrained readout rows, so training these rows with their own learning rate may speed up adaptation. Third, measuring weight drift in every layer (Figure C.6) would show whether each component, like the readout, settles on its own schedule.

sections.content: sustained training across rare localized midtraining peak strong early, weaker late weak early, stronger late residual category In the Pythia dictionaries, the 5121.6k reorganization window is where early-peaking features decay rather than where features peak. Peaks cluster at steps 16128 and, in Pythia-160M and 1B, again late in training, with at most 2% inside the window. Features that peak by step 128 keep mean ρf of at least 0.98 through step 256, which falls by step 3k to 0.29 in Pythia-160M and 0.63 in Pythia-1B as total decoder norm mass also falls. Figure D.1: The four selected cross-snapshot sparse dictionaries contain persistent and late-emerging features, with substantial early-decaying shares in Pythia-160M and Pythia-1B. Sharply transitional mid-training peaks are rare, so readout features do not follow single monotone growth pattern. Bars give the share of active features in each rule-based profile, and lines give each profiles median trajectory with interquartile bands. D.3 Late-Start Control for OLMo Few OLMo-2-7B features peak early and then decay, unlike those of the selected Pythia-160M and Pythia-1B dictionaries. Possible explanations include the missing OLMo-2-7B checkpoints before step 150, more monotone readout development, underrepresentation of weak early-only directions by checkpoint-spanning dictionary, and differences in tokenizer, data mixture, optimizer, and checkpoint spacing. To test the first, we fit Pythia-1B WU crosscoder on late-starting 32checkpoint schedule beginning at step 256, which removes the very early checkpoints but none of the other PythiaOLMo differences. Without the early checkpoints, the early-decaying profile almost vanishes, at 0.02% of late-start features (τ normalized over steps 256143k) against 24.1% in the selected Pythia-1B dictionary, whose own trajectories restricted to steps from 256 onward still give 25.4%. The profile therefore arises when the dictionary is fitted together with checkpoints near initialization, with the underlying Pythia model unchanged. Activation-rate definitions agree. sections.title: E WordNet Supersense Probe Analyses
sections.content: This appendix gives the protocol and results of the Pythia-160M WordNet analysis of Section 4.2 and its Pythia-1B replication. E.1 Probe Hyperparameters Each WordNet category is probed one-vs-rest on the mean-centered WU rows. Its positives are the categorys clean token ids, and its negatives are all other vocabulary rows, including the tokens of other categories, with class weights that balance the two classes. Each category uses one stratified split of vocabulary rows into two-thirds train and one-third held-out test, sampled with StratifiedShuffleSplit and run seed 0 [Pedregosa et al., 2011]. The split depends only on the labels and the seed, so each category keeps the same train and test rows at every checkpoint. This row split assigns token ids independently, so case and spacing variants of one lemma (dog, dog, Dog) can fall on both sides of it. Appendix E.6 repeats the probe with the split grouped by lemma. All other probe results in this appendix, including every figure and table, use the row split. Within the training split, an inner 3-fold stratified cross-validation selects {0.1, 1, 10}. The selected classifier is refit on the full training split and evaluated once on the held-out split. The reported WordNet analysis uses batched GPU implementation that matches LogisticRegression(solver=liblinear, class_weight=balanced) [Pedregosa et al., 2011] to within few thousandths in agreement checks, with max_iter=80. All reported probe values are held-out balanced accuracy. E.2 WordNet Supersense Inventory For each WordNet synset [Miller, 1995, Fellbaum, 1998], each one-word ASCII alphabetic lemma with length at least three is assigned to lexicographer file only if that file accounts for at least 60% of the lemmas synset occurrences. Each surviving lemma is mapped through five surface variants (lowercase and capitalized, each with and without leading space, and all capitals), and variant is kept only if it is single Pythia token. kept token is clean if, after its leading space is stripped, it decodes to at least three ASCII alphabetic characters and it has leading space, an initial capital, or all capitals, which excludes word-internal fragments. category is probed only if at least 20 clean token ids survive. This leaves 35 probed categories out of 45 WordNet lexicographer files. The skipped support-limited files are: adj.ppl (15 clean token ids), noun.Tops (13), noun.motive (3), noun.shape (9), verb.body (8), verb.competition (8), verb.consumption (11), verb.emotion (12), verb.perception (16), and verb.weather (1). Figure E.1: In Pythia-160M, all 35 WordNet supersense categories reach sustained decodability in the readout rows between steps 128 and 1000, and 33 have their largest adjacent-checkpoint gain in that interval. Rows are the 35 lexicographer-file categories with at least 20 clean token ids, in alphabetical order, and color is the held-out balanced accuracy of one-vs-rest linear probe on centered WU rows under the row split of Appendix E.1. Columns are the 32 Pythia checkpoints, equally spaced by index. The white box marks steps 512 and 1000, the checkpoints inside the 5121.6k reorganization window. E.3 Matched-Control Analysis matched-control analysis repeats the same probe procedure at all 32 Pythia-160M checkpoints. It compares observed WordNet labels with three controls. The metadata-only baseline is probe on token features alone. These are the log count of the token in held-out evaluation token set (not its training-corpus frequency), its character length, the norm of its centered row at the same checkpoint, spacing (whether the token begins with space), special-token status, and coarse token class (special, whitespace, lowercase, uppercase, or mixed-case alphabetic, digit, punctuation, other ASCII, or non-ASCII). The matched-random control replaces the category with tokens drawn from the same frequency, length, row norm, spacing, special-token, and token class bins, relaxing the match when bin is empty, and the label-shuffle control shuffles labels within these bins. The null probes draw new token sets and splits at every checkpoint. The matched-random and label-shuffle controls use 20 permutations per category and null type, so they are interpreted as confound check for this analysis. With 20 permutations the smallest attainable permutation p-value is 1/21 0.048, so 0.05 means that the observed accuracy beats all 20 null values. The 95th-percentile threshold used below interpolates between the two largest null values and is slightly less strict. 36 E.4 Probe Timing Trajectories categorys onset is the first checkpoint at which it reaches sustained decodability, meaning balanced accuracy of at least max(0.55, acc0 + 0.05) at that checkpoint and the next two. In Pythia-160M, lexical organization appears within short interval (Figure E.1). Onsets fall between steps 128 and 1000, 19 of them at step 256, and 33 of 35 categories have their largest adjacent-checkpoint gain in that interval, whose three adjacent pairs categorys largest gain would hit with probability 0.10 if it fell on uniformly random pair of the grid. Median probe accuracy starts near the matched-random and label-shuffle nulls at step 0, and with each categorys threshold set to the larger of its two 95th-percentile nulls, it exceeds the median threshold by 0.170 at step 512 and 0.272 at the final checkpoint. E.5 Pythia-1B Replication The timing replicates on the Pythia-1B WU trajectory, the model of the localization analysis in Section 4.4, with the same 35 categories and probe settings under the row split. Onsets range from step 128 to step 2000 with median of 512, and 33 of 35 categories have their largest gain in the four adjacent pairs from 128256 through 10002000, against 0.13 expected if each categorys largest gain fell on uniformly random pair. Neither the metadata-only baseline nor the matched-random and label-shuffle nulls were run on Pythia-1B, so these are observed probe accuracies only. E.6 Lemma-Grouped Splits Under the row split, 1199 of the 3249 positive test tokens (37%) have variant of the same lemma in the training split. We therefore rerun the probe with every vocabulary row grouped by its lowercased, space-stripped decoded string. The outer split is StratifiedGroupKFold with three folds and seed 0, holding out one fold as the test set, and the inner selection of uses the same grouped scheme on the training split. No positive lemma then appears on both sides. The categories, token ids, probe settings, and 32 checkpoints are unchanged, and each category keeps test support within one token of the row split. In Pythia-160M, median balanced accuracy rises from 0.500 at step 0 to 0.841 at the final checkpoint, against 0.874 under the row split. Of the 35 categories, 34 reach sustained decodability by step 1000, 33 still have their largest adjacent-checkpoint gain between steps 128 and 1000, and the median onset stays at step 256. The category that never separates is noun.relation, whose 24 token ids come from 14 lemmas. It stays at 0.500 at every checkpoint under the grouped split, so its accuracy under the row split came from variants of the same lemma falling on both sides of the split. Across split seeds 1 to 4, the median per-category difference between accuracy under the lemma-grouped split and under the row split is about 0.04 at the final checkpoint and lies within 0.005 at steps 256 and 512. In Pythia-1B, the median onset stays at step 512, onsets range from step 128 to step 1000, and one category never separates. The final median is 0.060 lower than under the row split. The matched-random and label-shuffle nulls and the metadata-only baseline were not rerun under the grouped split. Against the Pythia-160M nulls computed under the row split, 32 of 35 categories under the lemma-grouped split exceed both 95th percentiles at step 512, and 34 do from step 1000 to the final checkpoint.

sections.content: This appendix extends the probe and readout comparison to broader suite of 20 task families over 24 checkpoints of Pythia-1B and Pythia-6.9B. The 32-checkpoint logistic probe trajectories for SVA and IOI are in Figure F.1. Measurements. All measures read the final normalized hidden state. The 32-checkpoint SVA and IOI trajectories use the sweep Benv and the broader task suite uses Bho (Appendix A.3), and both exclude the native and terminal readouts, so neither need exceed E. Most open-vocabulary families have no shared binary label, so Table F.3 reports them by expression only. The BLiMP (Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs) anaphor and determinernoun agreement families do have one, and Appendix F.4 uses the anaphor family as contrast case. 37 Figure F.1: In the 32-checkpoint Pythia-6.9B trajectories for SVA (n = 320) and role-balanced IOI (n = 2,000), the logistic hidden state probe reaches high accuracy before native contrast accuracy rises, and on SVA the best swept readout tracks the native one. All three curves in panel use the same task inventory, and panel compares the probe with the strongest prompt-token or Gaussian-feature control. F.1 Prompt Construction The tasks of Table 1 and the other binary families of the broader task suite are built from fixed templates and word lists, and every item has correct answer and foil that are both single tokens with leading space. The prompt stops where the answer would begin, and we score the margin at its last token. Table F.1 gives the templates. The availability task suite and the localization items were built separately, with different templates for IOI and numeric comparison. Availability task suite. Simple agreement crosses 20 noun lemmas (key, book, student, and others) in singular and plural form with eight fixed prepositional phrases whose nouns are singular (to the cabinet, near the wall, and six more), so every plural subject is followed by singular attractor. The across-PP set pairs each singular item with plural item that has the same head lemma and verb pair. Its heads are 30 person nouns, its prepositions are by, near, beside, behind, next to, across from, and in front of, its attractors are singular place and object nouns or plural person nouns, and its answers come from 12 verb pairs; head and attractor number differ in 966 of 2,000 items. The relative clause sets follow the constructions of Marvin and Linzen [2018]. They use 20 person nouns as heads and attractors (never the same noun twice in one item), six relative clause verbs, and five main verb pairs (likes/like, runs/run, knows/know, writes/write, reads/read). The two sets contain the same 1,200 combinations of head, attractor, and verbs and differ in clause structure, so the clause verb agrees with the head in subject relative clause and with the attractor in an object relative clause. Role-balanced IOI uses two of 22 single-token first names and one of eight objects. For each name pair and object it produces both role orders, with filler sentence naming the recipient (Jane waited.), so the two prompts of pair contain the same tokens and only their order marks the answer. The three numeric sets use the same 1,000 unordered pairs of the numbers 2 to 99, each in both orders, so the correct answer comes first in half of the comparison items and True is correct in half of the true/false items. IOI takes every ordered pair of the 22 names once, with random object, in the template without the filler sentence, so the recipient is always the second name, and all 462 pairs pass the norm filter. The builder draws 2,000 ordered pairs of numbers from 2 to 99 without repeating draw, but both orders of pair give the same item, so an item can occur twice, and each of the at most 97 prompts recurs with different smaller numbers. Relational facts keep the 26 of 30 country and capital pairs that pass the single-token and norm filters. The foil is the first other capital in fixed list that passes the filters, which makes Paris the foil for most items, so this family largely contrasts each capital with one token. 38 Splits. sections.title: G Behavioral and Intervention Readout Checks
sections.content: This appendix documents the corpus-level readout swaps and the sparse feature interventions behind Section 4.4. Swaps exchange WU while keeping hidden states and targets fixed, and feature ablations remove selected reconstructed contributions to WU rows; neither intervenes on upstream circuits. G.1 Swap Grid Setup and Aggregate Measures The readout-swap grid evaluates Pythia-1B on fixed held-out corpus of 173,229 next-token predictions. Recipe Control: Readout Learning Rate and Developmental Timing This appendix details the controlled training experiment summarized in Section 4.5. H.1 Setup and Conditions The control trains four Pythia-architecture models of 31M parameters that share initialization seed and sequential data order, on 10B tokens. The conditions differ only in one of two recipe factors. Three vary the learning rate multiplier applied to the output readout WU (embed_out.weight): wu_lr_0p25 (0.25), baseline (1), and wu_lr_4x (4). The fourth, warmup_short, shortens the learning rate warmup (from the baseline 1430 steps to 715) at the baseline 1 readout learning rate. Each condition has one pretraining run and three crosscoder fits (seeds 0, 1, and 2). Crosscoder tables and figures show seed 0, and the timing statistics are reported for all three fits. fifth run with fourfold longer warmup (5720 steps) was also trained. Its warmup exceeds the 4769-step budget, so it never reaches the peak learning rate, and we leave it out of the comparison; its checkpoints are released with the others. The models use the Pythia architecture at dmodel = 256 with six layers and the Pythia tokenizer. Training follows Pythias optimizer recipe: AdamW [Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019] with (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.95), ϵ = 108, weight decay 0.1 (excluding LayerNorm parameters and biases), gradient clipping at 1.0, fp16 mixed precision, and global batch of 1024 sequences of 2048 tokens (2.1M tokens per step). The learning rate warms up linearly to peak of 103 over 1430 steps and follows Pythias cosine schedule over 143k steps, stopped at the 10B-token budget (4769 steps). At that point the learning rate is still within 0.2% of its peak, so the reported final losses precede any decay of the learning rate. The data are the first 10B tokens of Pythias preshuffled, pretokenized Pile [Gao et al., 2020, Biderman et al., 2023] (EleutherAI/pile-standard-pythia-preshuffled), in 2048-token blocks read once, in Pythias released order, by all conditions; the last 256 blocks (about 0.5M tokens) are held out for validation loss. The control keeps = 16 checkpoints at steps {0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 2479, 4096, 4769}, that is, step 0, the powers of two up to 4096, the final step, and one checkpoint that the trainer saved when the first 11-hour job slot ended. That slot checkpoint falls at step 2479 for baseline and at steps 2464 to 2481 across the four conditions, and we write it as 2479 throughout. The hidden state views of Appendix H.4 use held-out Pile tokens that directly follow the 10B-token training prefix in the same preshuffled order. The readout swap scores all 118,726 next-token positions of 120k-token slice, and the frequency class probe uses 20,000 positions sampled (seed 0) from 400k-token slice. Every WU trajectory crosscoder is fitted using the main Pythia-160M recipe of Table B.2 (mapped to dmodel = 256): JumpReLU, dSAE = 8192, λ1 = 0.3, learning rate 5 105, centered and scaled inputs, 300 epochs. Related Work, Limitations, and Broader Impact I.1 Extended Related Work Encoded but unexpressed information. Probes test what is decodable from representations [Alain and Bengio, 2016, Conneau et al., 2018, Hewitt and Manning, 2019, Tenney et al., 2019], and control tasks separate what the probe itself learns [Hewitt and Liang, 2019, Belinkov, 2022]. Trained models can encode answers that their outputs do not express [Burns et al., 2023, Orgad et al., 2025, Gekhman 50 et al., 2025], and training can make progress that loss and error metrics do not reveal [Barak et al., 2022]. We follow this gap across pretraining checkpoints and use readout swaps on fixed hidden states to attribute its expression side to the readout. Feature correspondence. Within fixed tokenizer, token identity gives our dictionary its row correspondence, but it does not remove hidden space reparameterizations or establish semantic identity across independently trained models [Ainsworth et al., 2023], and shared indices do not establish that the features are canonical units [Leask et al., 2025, Minder et al., 2025]. The checkpoint schedules bound temporal resolution, since they sample Pythia densely only before step 10k and each 31M run at 16 checkpoints. Profile shares and the median feature peak step depend on dictionary width and sparsity (Appendix D.5), so we read the shares qualitatively and compare timelines only at matched settings, whereas the reorganization window holds in 20 of 21 fits. The probes are linear and read only the final hidden state at the answer position, so they can miss distinctions decodable only nonlinearly or at other positions and layers. The comparisons have narrow scope. OLMo-2-7B is the only cross-family check, the sparse interventions use one configuration (Section 4.4), and tokenization, preprocessing, and optimization shape all comparisons. I.3 Implications Open questions. It remains open how task directions become coupled to the readout late in training, since relative clause agreement and numeric comparison keep gaps that no evaluated readout closes, and how hidden state and readout updates are coordinated, since readout swap isolates only one of the three terms of Equation (1). Control through the readout. The directions that carry the agreement margin at one configuration (Section 4.4) make the readout compact intervention site, as steering generation through linear transformations of the output embeddings suggests [Han et al., 2024], and the side effects and persistence of such edits remain to be measured (Appendix I.4). I.4 Social Impact The work deploys no language model and does not propose validated safety evaluation procedure. The main positive impact is methodological transparency, because treating the learned readout as part of the measured system makes developmental claims in logit space easier to audit, and the analysis code is released to support auditing of the reported checkpoint comparisons. The main negative-use concern is more targeted readout manipulation, since sparse readout features can identify token-family directions that affect logits.
